# Capability example

Copy `example/` to `src/capabilities/<your-name>/`, run `npm run dev`, and reload the Chrome
extension. The build discovers `index.ts` automatically. The test harness also builds this fixture
in isolation.

Keep only the contributions and dependencies you need. When removing an index declaration, also
remove unused TypeScript files. Rename stable tool, Skill, Provider, Renderer, page, and template
IDs, along with the `example` and `example-model` message namespaces, to avoid conflicts. Import the
framework through `#sdk/*` and package files through relative `.js` paths.

| Learn how to | Start here |
| --- | --- |
| Define a tool and typed results | [table-tool.ts](table-tool.ts), [result.ts](result.ts) |
| Render an interactive card and offline export | [value-card.ts](value-card.ts) |
| Add pages, settings, and draft saves | [ui.ts](ui.ts), [ui.html](ui.html), [ui.css](ui.css) |
| Translate messages and model descriptions | [messages.ts](messages.ts), [model-messages.ts](model-messages.ts) |
| Implement a local deterministic provider and authentication | [deterministic-provider.ts](deterministic-provider.ts), [presets.ts](presets.ts) |
| Supply context and observe run events | [context-and-observer.ts](context-and-observer.ts) |
| Parse documents and embed Skills | [json-document-codec.ts](json-document-codec.ts), [skills.ts](skills.ts) |

The [capability guide](../../../../src/capabilities/README.md) covers registration, SDK boundaries,
and extension development. In this example, tools and renderers share `result.ts` and parse unknown
results before displaying them. `ui.ts` uses `createSettingsForm` to separate the submitted snapshot
from later edits. Templates, images, and `srcset` use package-relative paths; styles reuse the
[design system](../../../../docs/design-system.md).

## Test the example

```bash
npm test -- playwright extension-example.spec.mjs --workers 1
npm run typecheck
```

The first command builds this fixture in isolated source and tests its tool, interactive card,
settings saves, provider, context, documents, disposal and remounting, and export. It uses synthetic
data and a local provider. Use
[extension-example.spec.mjs](../../../browser/extension-example.spec.mjs) as a starting point for
your own package's integration tests. `typecheck` checks capabilities and dependency boundaries in
the actual source tree.

## Record the demo

[`tool-renderer-example.gif`](../../../../docs/images/tool-renderer-example.gif) was recorded from
the Chrome test above using only this package's synthetic data. To record it again:

```bash
QINGZHOU_RECORD_DEMO=1 npm test -- playwright tests/browser/extension-example.spec.mjs --workers=1
```

Playwright saves `video.webm` under `tests/results/playwright/`. Convert it to a GIF at 8 fps and
760 px wide with palettegen/paletteuse. Check that the card is expanded and its result changes from
12 to 24 before replacing the public recording.

# Result selection example

Install this directory as a Skill or copy its files into a Skill created in qz. Load
`result-selection-example` and call `result_selection_example__choose` with `{"timeout":10}`.
Select one or more cards, then choose **Research selected roles**. The tool returns the selected
records to the Agent. The sample vacancies are synthetic and require no network access.

Replace the script's `items` with your collected results and keep each `id` stable. See the
[authoring guide](../../../../docs/skill-result-selection.md) for the renderer contract.

# qz

An open-source browser agent for humans and coding agents.

qz is a local-first extension for Chrome and Edge. This CLI and its MCP endpoint let coding agents
such as Claude Code, Codex, and pi drive your own browser, with your existing logins, or hand qz a
whole web task. Driving the browser needs no model configured in qz: your agent writes a short
script, and qz returns a compact result and trace that keep its token use low. People can watch
and step in from the side panel. Everything runs locally.

[Website](https://alibaba.github.io/qz-browser-agent/) ·
[GitHub](https://github.com/alibaba/qz-browser-agent) ·
[Chrome Web Store](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/dknbdgkgoinlgjpfebapkklbmjjgdblm) ·
[Full CLI and MCP reference](https://github.com/alibaba/qz-browser-agent/blob/main/docs/cli.md)

## Quick start

Requires Node.js 22 or later.

1. **Install the extension.** Click **Add to Chrome** on the
   [Chrome Web Store](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/dknbdgkgoinlgjpfebapkklbmjjgdblm).
2. **Install the CLI.** Or use `npx qz-browser-agent@latest` in place of `qz`.

   ```bash
   npm install --global qz-browser-agent@latest
   ```
3. **Drive the browser.** No model setup is needed in qz.

   ```bash
   qz session create --title "Read example page"
   qz script --session SESSION_ID - <<'JS'
   const page = qz.tab(await qz.openTab({ url: "https://example.com" }));
   return await page.read({ limit: 2000 });
   JS
   ```

   The first command connects the browser automatically. To teach your agent the full workflow,
   install the qz Skill with `npx skills add alibaba/qz-browser-agent -g`, or have it read `qz skill`.
4. **Or hand qz the whole task.** Choose a provider and model in the side panel's **Settings**, then:

   ```bash
   qz create "Find this year's Nobel Prize winners in every category and put them in a table with source links." --stream
   ```

   `--stream` shows progress, any questions qz needs you to answer, and the final result.

## Drive the browser

```bash
qz skill
qz session create --title "Read example page" --json
qz script --session SESSION_ID task.js --args '{"query":"example"}'
qz session show SESSION_ID
qz session cancel SESSION_ID
```

`session create` starts no model. With `--json`, `result.qz_skills` lists the Skills the new session
can use right away, and `qz.call("load_skill",{name})` makes another Skill's tools callable at once.

Scripts run outside pages and use the `qz` SDK. Bind `qz.tab(tabRef)` for page operations,
use `page.locator(query)` for element actions and waits, and `page.evaluate(code,args?)` for DOM access.
Discover additional capabilities with `qz.listTools()` or `qz.listTools({names:["list_images"]})`,
then invoke them through `qz.call(name,args)`. stdout is JSON `{ok,result,trace}`: execution status, the returned business value,
and ordered error and `trace()`/`console` messages without levels. Failures put `ToolError` in `result`; `undefined`
returns become `null`.

Browser operations prepare their connection automatically: they reuse the first responding
online browser, or open the connection page once in the system default browser. When qz does not respond
there, the page links to the Chrome Web Store and shows its URL with a copy button for a browser that has qz.
Select an existing profile with --client NAME|UUID; it never falls back to another profile. An incompatible
local service is restarted once before browser operations. Complete the extension’s connection
prompt when needed.

## Connect an MCP client

Print the MCP URL; this starts the local service if needed:

```bash
npx qz-browser-agent@latest mcp
```

The default is `http://127.0.0.1:18765/mcp`; use the URL your command prints if the port differs.

**Codex** (`~/.codex/config.toml`):

```toml
[mcp_servers.qz]
url = "http://127.0.0.1:18765/mcp"
```

**Claude Code**:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http qz http://127.0.0.1:18765/mcp
```

**Clients with an `mcpServers` JSON config**, such as Cursor:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "qz": { "url": "http://127.0.0.1:18765/mcp" }
  }
}
```

CLI and MCP share the same browser connection. The default MCP catalog is the direct-drive set;
`qz mcp --profile full` prints the URL for the task and diagnostic catalog. The MCP tool list is in the
[reference](https://github.com/alibaba/qz-browser-agent/blob/main/docs/cli.md#task-and-resource-operations).

## Common commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `qz connect uri` | Print a URL to open in a chosen browser profile |
| `qz status` | Check the connection and service address |
| `qz cleanup` | Stop registered local services and remove runtime files and logs |
| `qz browsers` | List paired browsers, or `forget` an offline one |
| `qz create "PROMPT"` | Start a task; add `--stream` or `--wait` to follow it |
| `qz send TASK_ID "MESSAGE"` | Send a follow-up, or `--steer` the current run |
| `qz tasks` | List tasks |
| `qz show TASK_ID` | Read a task's status, response, or pending question |
| `qz watch TASK_ID` | Follow a task until its work and queued messages finish |
| `qz submit` / `approve` / `reject` | Answer a question or permission request |
| `qz cancel TASK_ID` | Stop a task |
| `qz data` | List, export, or delete data tables |
| `qz images` | List, export, or delete image collections |
| `qz skills` | Find, read, or export Skills |
| `qz settings` | Read or update settings |
| `qz automations` | List or run automations |

With several browser profiles connected, choose one with `--client NAME|UUID` (or `-c`).
Run `qz COMMAND --help` for options. Interactive terminals show readable text; pipes receive JSON.

`watch`, `--wait`, and `--stream` follow the same task across runs until its current work and
accepted follow-ups and steering messages have completed and its queues are empty. Questions
and permission requests keep observation open. Task failure or stopping ends observation.
Timeout or Ctrl-C ends observation while the browser task continues; execute the returned
`watch` command with the same task ID and browser UUID to resume. Observation never resends messages.

## Privacy and local access

The service accepts connections only on your computer, and ordinary websites cannot use its MCP
endpoint. Local programs can control connected qz tasks while the service is running. Disconnect
a profile in its qz connection settings; task cancellation remains a separate operation.
Run `qz cleanup` to stop local services across installations and remove their runtime files and logs.
It preserves browser registrations, tabs, tasks and saved data; the next browser command starts its
service automatically. Active CLI requests and direct-drive scripts are interrupted; side-panel tasks
continue. `QZ_STATE_DIR` selects a different runtime directory when set.
Connection settings are stored in `~/.qz-browser-agent/run/`, and pairing credentials never
leave your computer.

## Reference

See the [qz CLI and MCP reference](https://github.com/alibaba/qz-browser-agent/blob/main/docs/cli.md)
for pairing a specific browser profile, Windows PowerShell notes, updates, task responses,
exports, output formats, exit codes, and the MCP tool mapping.

# Local conversation samples

Place qz HTML exports here to replay them with the current renderer. JSON files with a nonempty
`transcript` array are also supported; [stub.json](stub.json) shows the format. The benchmark treats
exports as recorded data and simulates Chrome APIs.

```bash
npm run benchmark -- conversation --real-examples
npm run benchmark -- conversation --real-examples --mode snapshot-render
npm run benchmark -- conversation --real-examples --mode stream-fixture-expanded
```

The runner reads `.html`, `.htm`, and `.json` files in filename order, with a fresh browser context
per sample. It skips subdirectories, symbolic links, hidden files, and `stub.json`. All samples run;
any failure or an empty corpus gives the command a failure status. Private samples are optional.

Reports default to `tests/results/conversation-real-examples/<timestamp>/`. `summary.json` records
each sample's status; `sample-N/` holds its evidence. Use `--artifact-dir` for another output root.
For single-file screenshots or baseline comparisons, pass a sample path directly.

Git tracks this README and the synthetic stub; other files and subdirectories are ignored. Keep real
conversations and their reports private, and review screenshots before sharing them.

For randomized scrolling and reading pauses, add `--stream-fuzz-seed 12345` to
`stream-fixture-interaction`. The runner checks completed tool cards each frame. Use different seeds
for repeated runs. The [test guide](../../../README.md#benchmarks-and-visual-checks) also covers
combined expansion, font-size, and viewport fuzzing. Keep its sample-path manifest in
`tests/results/`; this directory holds the conversation exports themselves.

# Privacy and browser permissions

This privacy policy covers the qz-browser-agent Chrome extension. qz stores its workspace in your
browser and connects to the model providers, websites, Skills, and MCP services you use for tasks.

## Information used by tasks

| Information | Use and destination |
| --- | --- |
| Prompts, conversations, attached files, and collected data | Stored locally; task context is sent to your configured model service to generate responses and choose actions. |
| Tab titles and URLs, page content, screenshots, and captured network data | Read for browser tasks. Tool results added to the task context are sent to the model service. Page and network content may contain personal or authentication information. |
| Bookmarks and browsing history | Read by their tools after Chrome grants access. Results used by a task are sent to the model service. |
| Location | Coordinates, accuracy, and timestamp are returned by `get_location` after first-use consent and sent to the model service for local information. |
| Model, Skill, and MCP credentials | Stored in your browser profile and used to authenticate requests to the corresponding configured services. |
| Screen recordings and exports | Created on request and saved locally. You choose whether to share the saved files. |

Skills can send task data to their configured services. Connected external agents receive tool
results and task data through MCP. Websites receive the requests, form submissions, and files
needed for the actions you request. Each receiving service applies its own privacy and retention
policy. Review those policies when choosing providers or enabling integrations.

## Storage and controls

Conversations, Skills, collections, and settings remain in your browser profile until you delete
them or clear the extension's storage. Diagnostic traces and cached resources are bounded by
storage limits. Delete chats, Skills, and collections from the side panel; remove configured
credentials in Settings. Uninstalling the extension removes its local storage. Downloaded files,
exports, and data already sent to other services are retained independently; delete those copies
at their destination.

You can stop a task, decline an access request, or disable the extension in Chrome. Chrome and your
operating system control device location access. Use HTTPS for remote model and integration
endpoints, and protect the browser profile that stores your settings and credentials.

## Limited Use

qz-browser-agent's use and transfer of information received from Chrome APIs adheres to the
[Chrome Web Store User Data Policy](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/webstore/program-policies/policies#protecting_user_privacy),
including the [Limited Use requirements](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/webstore/program-policies/limited-use).
Task data is used to provide the features you request.
qz does not sell this data or use it for advertising. Data sharing is limited to the services and
actions used to carry out your tasks, as described above.

For questions about this policy, contact the maintainers through the
[project issue tracker](https://github.com/alibaba/qz-browser-agent/issues). Share a description of
your question; keep credentials and personal task content out of public issues.

## Browser access

This guide explains the 19 permissions and host permission in [manifest.json](../src/manifest.json).
`history`, `bookmarks`, `desktopCapture`, and `downloads.open` are optional: Chrome requests them
when the user activates the feature. All other permissions, including `geolocation`, are declared
at installation. Chrome, operating system, and website restrictions still apply.

## Permission use

| Permission | Purpose and main callers | Feature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sidePanel` | Open the workspace; `background/service-worker.ts` and window commands | Core UI |
| `storage` | Store model settings, Sessions, Skills, and versioned repository records | Core state |
| `unlimitedStorage` | Persist conversations, documents, Data tables, and resources locally; disk space can still run out | Core state |
| `tabs` | Read URLs, titles, and status of task-owned tabs; `background/session/tabs.ts` | Page operations |
| `tabGroups` | Group task tabs; `shared/tab-groups.ts` | Task organization |
| `scripting` | Inject Content features and self-contained functions into task pages; `background/tools/runtime.ts` | Page operations |
| `debugger` | Use CDP to operate pages, capture screenshots, inspect requests, and print PDFs; `background/tools/cdp-runtime.ts` and tools | Page operations |
| `activeTab` | Access a page after user interaction and provide a screenshot fallback for the task's target; `capabilities/media/tools.ts` | Screenshots |
| `offscreen` | Bridge sandboxed scripts, keep background work alive, and convert images; `background/services/offscreen-document.ts` | Scripts and conversion |
| `alarms` | Schedule tasks, reminders, and background maintenance; `background/automation/runtime.ts` | Scheduling |
| `downloads` | Save files, documents, and exports; file tools, Artifacts, and export features | Files |
| `downloads.open` | Open saved files from Artifacts; `capabilities/sessions/artifacts/artifacts-feature.ts` | Files |
| `desktopCapture` | Let the user choose a screen or window when recording a case; `sidepanel/features/chat/case-recording-feature.ts` | Optional recording |
| `geolocation` | Serve the `get_location` tool after first-use consent; `background/services/location.ts` | Tool request |
| `bookmarks` | Search and manage bookmarks; `capabilities/bookmarks/tools.ts` | Optional tools |
| `history` | Search browsing history; `capabilities/bookmarks/tools.ts` | Optional tools |
| `clipboardWrite` | Copy answers, code, tables, and exported page content | UI actions |
| `notifications` | Show explicit reminders and task completion notifications; `background/services/chrome-notifications.ts` | Optional notifications |
| `declarativeNetRequest` | Apply provider headers and authorized Skill network rules to extension requests; `background/services/provider-header-rules.ts`, `background/skills/skill-network.ts` | Network access |
| `<all_urls>` | Run Content Scripts, browse across sites, and access user-configured provider and Skill endpoints | Host access |

Page tools require the Session's working tab or an explicitly authorized target. Tools, navigation,
fetch, MCP, and Skill resources also enforce shared safety checks. File URLs also require Chrome's
**Allow access to file URLs** setting.

To preview a generated HTML file, query `list_downloads` with its download ID and pass the returned
`fileUrl` to `open_tab`. The URL is available once the download completes and the file still exists.
Enable **Allow access to file URLs** in the extension details at `chrome://extensions` to open,
read, or interact with it. Each task reads the setting; if disabled, its system prompt tells the
Agent to avoid local file operations. Tools check access again before operating and return
`FILE_ACCESS_REQUIRED` when disabled.

Capabilities declare operations and UI; Background and Chrome enforce access. When removing a
feature from a distribution, review its callers, stored data, authorization checks, and manifest
together.

## On-demand access

History and bookmark tools pause with an authorization card in the side panel. Clicking **Allow
and continue** opens Chrome's permission request and resumes the tool after access is granted.
This wait is outside the tool execution timeout and ends when the task is stopped. MCP callers
must complete the same authorization in the side panel.

Firefox also requests the optional `userScripts` permission before executing page scripts
(`evaluate`, `wait_for_function`, and legacy page Skills). Click **Allow and continue** in the
qz sidebar, then accept Firefox's permission request. Firefox remembers the grant; revoking it
prompts again on the next use. Chrome uses its existing debugger permission.

Recording requests `desktopCapture` when the user starts recording. Opening a saved artifact
requests `downloads.open`; downloading files continues to use the required `downloads` permission.
Chrome remembers grants until the user revokes them. Subsequent use checks the current grant and
requests access again when needed.

## Denial and recovery

- Declining an optional permission cancels that action. Retry the feature to authorize it later.
- A failed `get_location` call keeps its error code and a short next step: allow browser location, turn on system Location Services, open the sidebar, or name a city or area. A disconnected sidebar asks them to open it in this window.
- Disabled notifications make the reminder tool return `SEND_ALERT_PERMISSION_DENIED`. Completion notifications leave the task's final state intact.
- Protected pages, closed tabs, and failed CDP attachment return tool errors. Select an authorized target before retrying.
- Chrome controls screen selection. Canceling its picker ends the recording attempt.
- A failed download or file open leaves the artifact in the Session so the user can try again.
- Storage exhaustion returns a persistence failure; report a successful save after the write commits.

## First-use disclosure

The Side Panel shows a localized data disclosure before initializing the workspace. **Agree and
continue** saves the current disclosure version and opens the normal landing screen. **Maybe later**
closes the panel and leaves consent unset. The next opening shows the disclosure again.

Background gates task commands and tool execution until consent is saved. Automation scheduling,
queued follow-up recovery, and MCP bridge polling start after consent. Storage failures keep the
panel on the disclosure so users can retry. This first-use consent is separate from the location
tool's consent and Chrome's optional permission grants.

## Data flow

Requests to the selected model provider contain user input and task context, possibly after
compaction. Context can include page and file content, screenshots, tab titles and URLs, and results
from authorized bookmark and history tools. When a task needs local information, the Agent can call
`get_location`. The first call explains that coordinates, accuracy, and the location timestamp will
be sent to the configured model service. A Side Panel click records consent in local storage;
later calls reuse it. Declining leaves consent unset. Device location access and an open Side Panel
are required; a failed lookup returns recovery guidance. History and bookmarks
are read when their tools are invoked; their authorization cards explain that task results are sent
to the configured model service. Skill network access and outgoing MCP connections follow user
configuration. After first-use consent, qz enables local MCP and CLI connections. Browser commands
prepare the local connection automatically; `qz connect uri` prints a URL for a chosen browser
profile. The extension verifies that page's address and the service identity before saving its
endpoint. It tries the saved endpoint (initially `http://127.0.0.1:18765`) and becomes idle after
three consecutive failures; the connection page resumes it. Local clients can then access qz tasks
and browser tools without a pairing token.
The service accepts loopback connections, validates request Host and Origin, and rejects ordinary
web-page origins. Disconnect a browser from its qz connection settings. See the [connection guide](../services/mcp-bridge/README.md)
for setup and connection controls.

Provider header rules use the current `chrome.runtime.id` as their `initiatorDomains` condition.
Background installs these session rules before accepting task and model configuration commands.
Worker restarts replace the provider rules and preserve the separate Skill rule namespace.

The Chrome Web Store privacy disclosures must describe location, website content, and other task
data sent to model services, alongside any enabled Skill or MCP data flows. Keep those disclosures,
the store listing, and this policy consistent with this behavior. Use this page's public URL as the
privacy policy URL in the Chrome Web Store Developer Dashboard.

Diagnostic traces stay local. Lifecycle observers receive frozen, redacted identity and phase
metadata. Users configure model endpoints, Skill sources, and outgoing MCP connections explicitly.

For permission semantics, see the [Chrome permission
list](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/permissions-list) and [Tabs
API](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/extensions/reference/api/tabs). When changing the manifest,
review this table, failure paths, and packaged Chrome tests together. Moving a feature to on-demand
permissions requires request, denial, revocation, and recovery flows.

# Tests

Run tests from the repository root. Default suites use synthetic fixtures, isolated browser
profiles, and local services. See [Commands](../docs/commands.md#run-tests) for dependencies and
runner options.

## Run and filter tests

Install the locked browser binaries with `npx playwright install chromium`. Playwright and extension
tests use Chromium; standalone page fixtures also use Chromium Headless Shell. Python browser tests
use `tests/python/uv.lock` through uv. Missing dependencies fail the run. The Firefox suite needs
Mozilla Firefox 154 or newer and Chromium Headless Shell for its DOM unit fixtures:
`npx playwright install --with-deps chromium-headless-shell firefox`.

```bash
npm test -- unit contracts
npm test -- unit --match session
npm test -- browser --list
npm test -- playwright renderer-lifecycle.spec.mjs --workers 1
npm run verify
npm run verify:chrome
npm run verify:firefox
```

| Suite | What it checks |
| --- | --- |
| `unit` | Logic, repositories, cancellation, concurrency and data formats |
| `contracts` | Side Panel projections, Port lifecycle and cross-context messages |
| `services` | Node MCP/CLI lifecycle, endpoint failures, and Agent acceptance checks |
| `browser` | Playwright, Python page smoke tests and Data Grid behavior |
| `e2e` | The loaded extension, Session exchange, documents and tool timelines |
| `release` | Deterministic builds, ZIP contents and the packaged extension |
| `visual` | Tool timelines and conversation streaming in Chromium |
| `firefox` | Firefox unit tests and Playwright in Mozilla Firefox against `dist/extension-firefox/` |

`firefox` is not part of `npm test` or `--all`. `npm run verify:firefox` runs it. `browser`, `e2e`,
`release`, and `visual` load the Chrome package. `npm run build:firefox` writes the production package
in `dist/extension-firefox/` and does not run this suite.

`npm test` selects `unit contracts services browser`. `--all` selects those shared suites plus `e2e`,
`release`, and `visual`. `npm run verify` type-checks and runs `unit`, `contracts`, and `services`.
`npm run verify:chrome` runs the Chrome package suites. `npm run verify && npm run verify:chrome`
type-checks and runs the shared suites plus the Chrome package suites. `npm run verify:coverage`
type-checks and runs `--all` with coverage gates.

## Direct-drive CLI fuzzing

Run the connection state-machine corpus and the actual CLI/browser task corpus separately:

```bash
npm test -- unit --match qz-connection-fuzz
npm test -- playwright direct-drive-fuzz.spec.mjs --workers 2
```

The corpus contains **50 distinct scenario types**, not 50 seeds: 25 connection scenarios and
25 browser task scenarios. Both manifests assert their count and uniqueness.

The [connection corpus](unit/test-qz-connection-fuzz.mjs) uses four persisted seeds and a stateful
simulated transport. Each seed shuffles all 25 scenarios twice, producing 200 transitions by
default. It varies browser identities, registration order, session ownership, disconnections,
compatibility upgrades, service replacement, cancellation, and lost mutation replies. Additional
histories cover default-browser connection/pending, reconnect deadline exhaustion, cancellation during
startup/upgrade, and transcript-only ownership discovery/conflicts. It checks routing and rejects
ambiguous ownership without dispatching a mutation. This layer does not launch browsers or test
installation of a released CLI version. The separate stalled-health regression in
`test-qz-client-scope.mjs` uses real HTTP to check cancellation and remaining connection budgets.

The browser corpus launches two isolated Chromium profiles against one real bridge and executes
the CLI bin in a fresh subprocess for every command. Each of three persisted seeds runs all 25
scenarios: ordinary, SPA and open-shadow checkout; parallel document comparison; and the 21
[additional tasks](support/drive-task-scenarios.mjs). These check missing/unknown references,
detached UIDs, reload/hash/document navigation, exactly-once AJAX triggers, popup chains, alias
reuse/collisions, foreign-session writes, preservation of read-only user tabs, same-tab serialization,
cross-tab progress, caught errors, cancellation, timeout without replay, Unicode business values,
large-result projection, catalog recovery, and iframe target identity.
Histories vary task order, owning profile, values, action order, and
failures before or after submission. Service restarts occur before submission, after submission,
or while the response to a recorded submission is withheld. The test observes automatic
reconnection with the same browser identities, then resumes the same session without replaying
the submission. Server receipts and independent Playwright DOM reads verify results and cleanup.
Compatible build differences use the real daemon discovery path; incompatible upgrade admission
is covered by the simulated corpus. These new browser cases do not cover Firefox or Edge.

Filter a persisted case with `--grep 'seed=65537'`. Set `QZ_DRIVE_FUZZ_SEEDS` to comma-separated
positive uint32 seeds to explore more browser histories, or `QZ_CONNECTION_FUZZ_SEEDS` to uint32
seeds for the simulated corpus. Playwright attaches `direct-drive-fuzz.json` with scenario IDs,
outcomes, command ranges, generated tasks, fault phases, scripts, CLI output, elapsed times, and
output character counts. Additional tasks use fresh Sessions and are all attempted even if an
earlier task fails; any failed task still fails the seed. The browser tests
also compare full element observations with returned target maps and check that intermediate
results do not leak into stdout. Explicit script values above 48,000 characters remain intact;
scripts can return a compact projection instead. Character counts measure transport volume, not model tokens.
Neither corpus invokes a model or measures model-driven task success rates.

final answer. It also pairs the current CLI bridge and lists both tasks through the real CLI/MCP
path. Set `QINGZHOU_FIREFOX_EXTENSION_DIR` to a built Firefox extension, `FIREFOX_EXECUTABLE` to
a supported Firefox, and `QINGZHOU_LIVE_REPORT` for the JSON evidence. A test-only loopback
forwarder uses Node's network configuration to reach DeepSeek, preserving request payloads and
forwarding upstream SSE chunks. Production packages contain neither forwarding nor probe scripts.

For the extended session-management checks, run `live deepseek` with
`QINGZHOU_LIVE_SESSION_MANAGEMENT=1 QINGZHOU_LIVE_SESSION_MANAGEMENT_EXTENDED=1`. The ordinary
lifecycle run and this management run use separate temporary profiles. Set `QINGZHOU_LIVE_REPORT` to
an output JSON path for `live deepseek` or `live rate` to retain success and failure evidence; the
parent directory must already exist.

Use `QINGZHOU_LIVE_CASES=workerRestart` to run a four-turn conversation, close the panel and stop
the Worker during the third turn, then verify checkpoint recovery and continue the same chat.
The report includes recovered transcripts, request counts, and screenshots when
`QINGZHOU_LIVE_REPORT` is set.

Key precedence is an explicit key file (`--ak-file` / `--key-file` or the corresponding file
variable), the provider environment variable, then root `.env.local`. The explicit live invocation
loads the chosen key into a temporary profile and removes that profile on exit.

Add `--capture-dir tests/results/agent/captures` to save each case's transcript, acceptance evidence
and Data readback, including failed cases. Credentials are redacted before writing. Validate actual
business results through page state, stored data, and tool output.

```bash

  --cases goal_driven_pagination,document_pipeline,parallel_subtasks --concurrency 2 \
  --capture-dir tests/results/agent/ja/captures --report tests/results/agent/ja/report.json
```

Run the focused DeepSeek vision regression against a local canvas in an isolated Chrome profile:

```bash

node --import tsx tests/live/deepseek-vision.mjs --steps 30
```

It uses `deepseek-flash` by default (`QINGZHOU_DEEPSEEK_MODEL` overrides it). The default nine-step
run checks the first image-window eviction; `--steps 30` exercises repeated evictions in one Agent
run. Every step requires a fresh screenshot and a correct visual click, with the 2560×1440 →
2048×1152 coordinate mapping and 2 MiB image limit checked independently. The canvas uses a fixed
viewport; scrolling has separate page-tool coverage. Redacted request counts, pruning checkpoints,
click evidence and a final screenshot are saved under `tests/results/deepseek-vision/` for nine
steps and its `retention-30/` subdirectory for thirty. The script removes its temporary profile on

```bash

```

## Benchmarks and visual checks

[Benchmarks](../docs/benchmarks.md) covers conversation replay, seeded scrolling, Data Grid,
Markdown streaming, Provider timing replay, production loading, CSS comparisons and article
extraction. Run the relevant synthetic benchmark for stream, motion, timeline or virtualized-grid
changes.

The browser tool-anchor viewport fuzz uses 60 fixed-seed cases across three windows and six font
sizes. Its streaming stage updates thinking text. The assistant viewport fuzz separately covers
six seeded streams with Markdown tables, long links and footnotes across three windows, light/dark
themes, tail following and history reading. Native clicks and wheels overlap randomized content
chunks and delivery delays. It records every frame through stream completion, rejects backward tail
motion even when the tail gap stays zero, and checks history anchors and final table/link semantics.
Coverage assertions require real inputs and changing content during the observed idle periods.

```bash

QINGZHOU_ASSISTANT_FUZZ_SEED_OFFSET=100000 npm test -- playwright \
  tests/browser/assistant-viewport-stability-fuzz.spec.mjs --repeat-each=3
```

`QINGZHOU_FUZZ_MARKDOWN_MODULE` points to a local compiled ESM renderer for negative-control runs;
normal verification always loads the current renderer. Keep baseline modules in ignored output.

```bash

  tests/browser/viewport-stability-fuzz.spec.mjs --repeat-each=3 --workers=1
```

Paths may be absolute or relative to the repository. Each seed is reproducible; evidence goes to the
Playwright case output. Keep the path list in `tests/results/`; `real_examples/` holds conversation
exports. Geometry tests cover layout changes; transient operating-system/GPU flicker still needs

# Qingzhou for DeepSeek Harness

[中文](README.zh-CN.md)

Use Qingzhou (轻舟) to operate your connected Chrome, Edge or Firefox from dsh. The
`qz_browser` tool runs scripts through the installed `qz` CLI. Results, authored traces,
scripts and screenshots appear in a compact conversation card that follows dsh's theme.

## Install

Requires Node.js 24.9 or later, dsh `0.2.2-rc.1`, and a matching qz CLI and browser extension.
Install [Qingzhou](https://alibaba.github.io/qz-browser-agent/), open its side panel once,
and complete setup.

```sh
npm install --global qz-browser-agent
qz --version
```

After this package is published, install it into the profile you use:

```sh
dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-browser-qz
```

You can also install the package from dsh's Plugins page. Installation enables its bundle;
restart dsh when the installer requests it. For a local package, replace the package name
with the absolute path to the `.tgz` produced by `npm pack` below.

Ask dsh to use Qingzhou to read a page or complete a browser task. The CLI prepares the
connection automatically. For another browser profile, run `qz connect uri` and open the
printed URL in that browser.

## Browser scripts

The model calls `qz_browser` with a short `title`, JavaScript `code`, optional JSON `args`,
and a `timeout` in seconds. The plugin creates and retains the browser session for the
conversation. Browser operations use the qz SDK:

```js
const opened = await qz.openTab({ url: "https://example.com", tabAlias: "example" });
const page = qz.tab(opened);
trace("Opened the example page");
return await page.read({ limit: 2000 });
```

Later calls reuse `qz.tab("example")`. Use `page.goto(url)` to navigate the same tab,
`page.locator(query)` for actions, and `page.evaluate(fn, args)` for page DOM access.
Independent page workflows can use `Promise.all` inside one script. The plugin serializes
separate calls in the same conversation.

Return the data the next step needs. To show a screenshot, include its receipt in the return
value, for example `return { screenshot: await page.screenshot() }`. The adapter attaches
images exported by the CLI to the dsh result. Merely capturing an image without returning
it does not attach it. The model receives `{ok,result,trace}` and image attachments;
the card displays the same result and trace. Trace contains script-authored messages and errors.

Return the complete `page.read()` or `page.axTree()` result to retain its presentation, including
inside an object such as `{ article, structure }`. Articles render Markdown with their title and
source; page structure separates roles, names and targets, with collapsible branches. Screenshots
and `read_image` results use image previews that open the original, with dimensions and format.
Raw values remain available through Inspect and Copy. Ordinary Markdown tables render as tables;
embedded HTML, including complex merged-cell tables, is shown as text by dsh's Markdown renderer.

Stopping a running call interrupts that script and retains its session and tabs. Completed
browser actions are not rolled back. Resuming the same dsh conversation retains its binding;
a fork gets its own browser session. If the qz session has ended or expired, the call reports
that fact before executing the script, and the next call can open fresh task pages.

## Configuration

Defaults use `qz` from `PATH` and the CLI's normal connection settings. Optional overrides
belong to the `browser-qz` entry in your profile patch:

```yaml
- id: browser-qz
  config:
    cliPath: /absolute/path/to/qz
    client: work-browser
```

`cliPath` can also point to `services/mcp-bridge/src/bin.mjs` in a qz checkout. `stateDir`
selects a separate qz state directory when needed; leaving it unset shares the ordinary CLI
service. `client` selects a paired browser by its name or UUID. Use `qz browsers` to list them.
On Windows, use the npm-installed CLI or its JavaScript entry so cancellation can reach the CLI.

## Develop and package

From this directory:

```sh
npm ci
npm test
npm run build
npm run check:package
```

`check:package` packs, installs in a temporary directory, checks both entry points, and writes
the tested tarball to `dist/`. `npm pack` also builds a tarball directly.
The tarball contains the host adapter, the built dsh client, bundle configuration, locale
metadata and documentation. Installation runs no build script. `npm pack` builds the client
locally; React and dsh services are supplied by the host. The browser extension and CLI are
separate installations.

The source package is in `services/dsh-plugin`. Keep its dsh peer versions aligned with the
version used for integration checks. Review the package contents and set the intended version
before publishing with `npm publish --access public`.

# qz CLI and MCP reference

Run browser tasks, manage results, and connect external agents to qz through CLI or MCP.
For a short overview, see the [package README](../services/mcp-bridge/README.md).
Requires Node.js 22 or later. CLI and MCP share one local daemon. Each paired browser profile
has its own connection.

The daemon is [`services/mcp-bridge`](../services/mcp-bridge/README.md). From this repository the
command is `npm run qz`. The published command is `qz`. The daemon is not copied into
`dist/extension/` or `dist/extension-firefox/`. Chrome loads the first directory. Firefox loads
the second. Package layout is in [Firefox packaging](firefox-packaging.md). The command list is
in [Commands](commands.md).

## Quick start

The examples and suggested next commands use `qz`. Replace it with

## Load qz in Firefox

One daemon serves both packages. Build the Firefox package and load it for this session.
Pairing uses **Connect CLI** or a pairing URL.

```bash
npm run build:firefox
```

`npm run dev:firefox` watches `dist/extension-firefox/` and leaves `dist/extension/` alone.
Load `dist/extension-firefox/manifest.json` from `about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox`. The
clicks, the reload, and the fact that a temporary add-on is removed when Firefox exits are in
[Load temporarily in Firefox](commands.md#load-temporarily-in-firefox). The gecko id
`qz-browser-agent@heleifz.github.io` and the Chrome `key` are compared in
[Firefox packaging](firefox-packaging.md#identifiers).

Open the sidebar from the toolbar button, then pair:

1. In qz, open **Settings → Advanced → CLI → Connect CLI**. The service address is the one
   `qz status` prints. The default is `http://127.0.0.1:18765`.
2. Or run `qz connect uri --json` and open `result.url` in the Firefox profile that has
   the add-on. The URI command does not open a browser.

The settings sender accepts a `moz-extension://<host>/` page when `sender.id` is this add-on.
A web page URL is rejected.

The daemon allows two Origin shapes on extension routes
([`services/mcp-bridge/src/server.mjs`](../services/mcp-bridge/src/server.mjs)). A Chrome origin
remains `chrome-extension://` plus 32 characters from `a` to `p`. A Firefox origin is
`moz-extension://` plus a lowercase UUID. Firefox stores that UUID for gecko id
`qz-browser-agent@heleifz.github.io` in the profile pref `extensions.webextensions.uuids`.
`runtime.id` stays the gecko id. The bridge cannot derive the UUID from the gecko id, so the
origin check accepts the UUID shape and then the pairing token authenticates the profile.
The first `/v1/qingzhou/pair` from an allowed origin issues or checks that token. Later poll
and result calls require it. A web origin is rejected with `403` and `invalid bridge origin`.
A request to `/mcp` that carries any Origin is rejected. The daemon still binds to loopback.

1. Run `npm run build:firefox`. In Firefox 154 or later, open

2. Open the sidebar and accept the data notice.
3. Run `npm run qz -- connect uri --json` and open `result.url` in that Firefox window.

## Connection preparation

```bash
qz session create --title "Inspect a page"
qz status
qz browsers
qz mcp
```

Browser operations reuse a responding connection or prepare one automatically. The local service
prefers port 18765; if another program owns it, the service chooses a free port. `status` shows the
actual service address, and `mcp` prints its MCP URL. A protocol-incompatible service is restarted
once under its scope lock after verifying its process and instance identity. Build changes alone
do not restart compatible services. No submitted browser operation is replayed during recovery.

Without an explicit selection, a new task uses the first responding browser. An existing session
is located through read-only queries when several browsers are online; ambiguous ownership requires
`--client NAME|UUID`. An explicit selection never falls back to another browser. With no online
connection, the CLI opens the connection page once in the system default browser and waits there.
When the service confirms a browser is reconnecting, the CLI first waits for its lease recovery within
the command's timeout. If connection remains pending, check that page or use `qz connect uri` to pair
a chosen browser profile. Pairing requires the extension’s first-use notice and connection prompt.
The connection page updates while reconnecting, then counts down for three seconds and closes after
a successful connection.

To disconnect one browser, click **Disconnect: NAME** in its qz Settings. To cancel a task, use
`qz cancel TASK_ID`, or `qz session cancel ID` for a direct-drive session, adding --client when needed.
The extension retains browser tasks independently of the local service.

Run `qz cleanup` to stop registered local services from installed packages and development checkouts,
and remove their runtime files and logs. It uses `~/.qz-browser-agent/run/`, or `QZ_STATE_DIR` when set.
Browser registrations, tabs, tasks and saved data are preserved. The next browser command starts
its service automatically. Active CLI requests and direct-drive scripts are interrupted; side-panel
tasks continue. Unverified or busy entries are reported and preserved; incomplete cleanup
exits with code 1. Use `--json` for the per-service report.

In a sandbox with isolated process IDs, the CLI can reuse a host service when its runtime files
and localhost endpoint are accessible. Start and connect the service from a host terminal first
with `qz connect uri`. Run service cleanup or upgrades from the host terminal when the sandbox
cannot verify the service process.

### Pair a selected browser from the shell

Print a pairing URL without opening a browser, waiting for a connection or interrupting tasks:

```bash
qz connect uri
qz connect uri --name work --json
```

The first command prints the URL. With --json, read result.url. Open that exact URL in the browser
profile where qz is installed. --name names a new profile; --client NAME|UUID addresses a registered
profile and cannot be combined with --name. To request a custom service port, use --port; if the
service is already running on another port, it remains running and the command reports its address.

### Open the URL in Chrome

Set `QZ_PAIRING_URL` to that URL and `QZ_PROFILE_DIRECTORY` to the selected profile's directory
name, such as `Default` or `Profile 2`. These are directory names, not Chrome's display labels.
Use a profile already chosen by the user. On macOS:

```sh
open -na "Google Chrome" --args --profile-directory="$QZ_PROFILE_DIRECTORY" "$QZ_PAIRING_URL"
```

For Chrome on Linux:

```sh
google-chrome --profile-directory="$QZ_PROFILE_DIRECTORY" "$QZ_PAIRING_URL"
```

For Chrome installed under Program Files on Windows, set `$QzProfileDirectory` and
`$QzPairingUrl` to those same values in PowerShell:

```powershell
& "$env:ProgramFiles\Google\Chrome\Application\chrome.exe" "--profile-directory=$QzProfileDirectory" $QzPairingUrl
```

Use the installed browser's executable or app name. For an existing custom data directory, also
pass `--user-data-dir` with its exact path; for example on macOS:

```sh
open -na "Google Chrome" --args --user-data-dir="$QZ_USER_DATA_DIR" --profile-directory="$QZ_PROFILE_DIRECTORY" "$QZ_PAIRING_URL"
```

The [Chrome profile documentation](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/master/docs/user_data_dir.md)
distinguishes the data directory from the profile inside it. A new data directory needs its own
extension installation and first-use setup.

### Open the URL in Firefox

A Firefox profile is the directory path shown in `about:profiles`. Load the temporary add-on in
that profile first. See [Load qz in Firefox](#load-qz-in-firefox).

```sh
firefox --profile "$QZ_FIREFOX_PROFILE" "$QZ_PAIRING_URL"
```

Use the installed Firefox executable when `firefox` is not on `PATH`. A new profile needs the
temporary add-on and first-use setup again. After the page opens, the sidebar background pairs
with the daemon. `qz browsers` lists that profile when the pair succeeds. See
[Check Connect CLI on a local Firefox](#check-connect-cli-on-a-local-firefox).

`--name work` adds `?name=work` to the URL. The profile opening it receives that identifier,
including when it already has a connection. Without `--name`, a registered profile keeps its name;
a new profile receives the next available name: `default`, `browser-2`, and so on. A name conflict
requires another name. `qz connect uri --name work` only prints the URL.
These URL-returning commands do not confirm that a browser connected. Verify it with:

```bash
qz browsers --json
qz create "Summarize the current page." --client UUID --stream
```

Read `result.browsers`, then use the intended online entry's `clientId` UUID. `--client` selects an
existing connection and cannot be combined with --name on the URI command. --port follows the
existing-service behavior above.

### Add and select browsers

You can also pair from **qz Settings → Advanced → CLI** in the intended profile. Enter a distinct
browser identifier and connect. Use the service address printed by `qz status` in **Local service address** if
its port differs from 18765. Names use 1–64 letters, digits, underscores, or hyphens, beginning with
a letter or digit; names are case-sensitive. UUID-shaped names are reserved for profile IDs.

```bash
qz browsers
qz create "Summarize the current page." --client work --stream
qz show TASK_ID --client work
qz data --client work
```

`--client NAME|UUID` and `-c NAME|UUID` select a profile. New tasks use the first responsive browser;
existing sessions are located through read-only queries when several browsers are online, and
ambiguous ownership requires a selection. `default` is a name, not a routing preference. An unknown
selection fails immediately; an offline selection waits for that UUID within the connection deadline
without opening or using another browser. Each command resolves its name once and carries the UUID through subsequent
requests. JSON task results and suggested next commands include that UUID.

Names remain registered while their browsers are offline and across service restarts. To release
an offline name, remove its registration explicitly:

```bash
qz browsers forget work
```

An online browser must first disconnect in its settings. Forgetting a registration leaves the
browser's tasks and data intact. A browser can then explicitly pair using the released name.

### Update the connection

Use the current CLI and extension together. Compatible running services remain in use after package
updates. Before browser operations, the CLI can replace a protocol-incompatible service once under
its scope lock, retaining the service address and paired identities. If the extension’s script API
is incompatible, update the CLI and extension together before retrying; no script is submitted.
Chrome store users update through the store; manual packages must be reloaded. Firefox development
packages are rebuilt with npm run build:firefox and reloaded at about:debugging.

## Connect an MCP client

Run `qz mcp` to start or reuse the local service. If the intended profile is not paired, open the URL
from `qz connect uri` there. Copy the MCP URL into your client’s HTTP configuration:

```toml
[mcp_servers.qz]
url = "http://127.0.0.1:18765/mcp"
```

Use the URL printed by your command if its port differs. `qz mcp --json` returns the URL as JSON
for scripts. The `qingzhou_*` MCP tool names and extension protocol remain available. Responses
to pending input bind to an explicit `waitId`. Use `qingzhou_bridge_status` to list browser names
and UUIDs, then pass `clientId: "work"` or a UUID to browser tools. Selection is required with
multiple online browsers. Task results include the resolved `clientId`. MCP initialization and streaming are handled by your
client's MCP implementation.

### Task and resource operations

CLI and MCP use the same task observer and browser operations. The task and resource commands map to these MCP operations:

| CLI | MCP tool |
| --- | --- |
| `browsers`, `browsers forget` | `qingzhou_bridge_status`, `qingzhou_forget_browser` |
| `create`, `send`, `cancel` | `qingzhou_create_session`, `qingzhou_send_message`, `qingzhou_stop_session` |
| `tasks`, `show`, `watch` | `qingzhou_list_sessions`, `qingzhou_get_session_snapshot`, `qingzhou_watch_task` |
| `show`, `submit` / `approve` / `reject` | `qingzhou_get_session_snapshot`, `qingzhou_respond_to_user_input` |
| `data list` / `delete` / `export` | `qingzhou_list_data_tables`, `qingzhou_delete_data_table`, `qingzhou_export_data_table` |
| `images list` / `delete` / `export` | `qingzhou_list_image_collections`, `qingzhou_delete_image_collection`, `qingzhou_export_image_collection` |
| `skills list` / `show` / `read` / `tools` / `export` | `qingzhou_list_skills`, `qingzhou_get_skill`, `qingzhou_get_skill_resource`, `qingzhou_list_plugins`, `qingzhou_export_skill` |
| `settings get` / `set` | `qingzhou_get_settings`, `qingzhou_update_settings` |
| `automations list` / `run` | `qingzhou_list_automations`, `qingzhou_run_automation` |

MCP creation, message submission, and input responses accept `wait: true` to observe the task until
its current work and accepted follow-ups and steering messages have finished. Observation follows
successive runs of the same task and succeeds when the task is completed and its queues are empty.
Messages accepted after that completion snapshot belong to later work.
`stream: true` also sends assistant text through standard MCP progress notifications. A watch call
uses the same completion condition and always waits. For example, call `qingzhou_create_session` with:

```json
{"firstMessage":"Summarize the current page.","stream":true}
```

Supply `_meta.progressToken` on the MCP request to receive progress. Each notification includes a
readable `message` and its structured event in `params._meta["qz/task-event"]`. Events include
`created`, `status`, `text`, `replace`, and `input`. Input events include the current form, exact
field IDs, option values, and `responseTemplate`. Fill that template and pass it to
`qingzhou_respond_to_user_input`; another CLI or MCP connection can answer while the original call
keeps waiting. A permission dialog the browser itself shows still needs a click in the side panel
or sidebar.

MCP `timeoutSeconds` bounds each browser request (180 seconds by default).
`waitTimeoutSeconds` bounds the whole observation; omit it for no overall deadline. Configure your
MCP client's own request deadline for long tasks. Task failure or stopping ends observation. On
timeout or cancellation, the browser task continues; execute the returned `qingzhou_watch_task`
recovery call with the same task and browser IDs to continue observing. Observation never resends
a message. `send_message` supports `steer: true`; its returned `clientMessageId` confirms acceptance
and sets the starting point for streamed responses, including within the same run. A long
observation stays bound to the browser selected when it started.

When a watched task is absent from the selected browser, `task_deleted` returns a
`qingzhou_list_sessions` recovery call for that same `clientId`. Check the task ID and browser
selection before watching again. The raw snapshot tool continues to return `session: null`
for a missing task.

## Run a task

```bash
qz create "Compare these two laptops."
qz create "Summarize the current page." --title "Research" --wait
qz create "Find the main differences between these pages." --stream
qz send TASK_ID "Add the source links." --stream
qz send TASK_ID "Focus on open-source options." --steer --stream
qz tasks
qz show TASK_ID
qz cancel TASK_ID
```

`create` starts a task and returns its ID. The title is optional. `--wait` follows the task through
its current work and accepted follow-ups and steering messages, including successive runs.
`--stream` also displays progress as it arrives. Both succeed when the task is completed and its
queues are empty. Both stay connected while the task waits for user input and continue automatically
after you respond. Task failure or stopping ends observation. Task observation has no default time limit.
Add `--timeout SECONDS` to set a total deadline, including time spent waiting for input. Each
individual connection request remains bounded (180 seconds by default). A timeout or Ctrl-C ends
watching. Run the returned `qz watch TASK_ID --stream --client CLIENT_UUID` recovery command to
resume observation of the same task in the same browser; `qz cancel TASK_ID` stops the task.

`show` JSON includes `usage` for the whole task. `create --wait`, `send --wait`, `watch`, and the other waiting commands include the same object on `snapshot.usage`. The fields are `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, `cachedTokens`, `costUsd`, `modelCalls`, `toolCalls`, `screenshots`, and `contextCompressions`. Token and cost totals sum the provider usage stored on each recorded model call, including context compression. `inputTokens` counts prompt tokens that were not read from cache, including tokens written into the cache. `cachedTokens` counts cache reads. `costUsd` is dollars reported by the provider (`cost_in_usd_ticks / 10^10`, or `cost_usd` when the provider reports dollars directly). A call that does not report a price adds zero. Sessions saved before this codec change did not keep cost fields, so `costUsd` is 0 for those historical calls. `toolCalls` counts tools that were invoked. `screenshots` counts completed successful calls whose name contains `screenshot`, and `act_on_screen` when it returns a screenshot. `contextCompressions` counts completed context compressions. `contextUsage` remains the latest context reading.

`show` returns `task_not_found` with exit code 1 when the selected browser has no matching task.
`watch` retains the `task_deleted` error code and directs you to `qz tasks --client CLIENT_UUID`.
Check the task ID and `qz browsers` before retrying; the task may have been deleted or belong to
another browser. Recovery commands keep the originally selected browser UUID.

Provide the task text directly after `create`, or read it from stdin with `qz create -`.
Use `--parent TASK_ID` to create a child task, and `qz tasks --limit N` to limit the task list.
`send TASK_ID MESSAGE` sends a follow-up to the specified task; `qz send TASK_ID -` reads the message
from stdin. A busy task queues a follow-up for its next run. Add `--steer` to deliver the message
to the current run at its next safe boundary. Both start a new run when the task is idle. Pending
questions and permissions still require a response.

The send response confirms acceptance and includes `clientMessageId`. `--wait` and `--stream`
follow the same task until its work is completed and its queues are empty. Removing an unconsumed
follow-up or steering message removes that work from the wait; observation can complete once the
remaining execution ends and the queues are empty. Streaming starts after the submitted message,
including when steering continues the same run, and follows later runs without repeating text.
Pending questions from the preceding run remain visible so you can answer them and let a queued
follow-up proceed. A connection failure never resends a message automatically.

## Respond to a task

```bash
qz show TASK_ID
qz submit TASK_ID '{"selectedIds":["option-a"]}' --stream
qz approve TASK_ID --wait
qz reject TASK_ID
qz watch TASK_ID --stream
```

`show` and pending-input notices include the current question, labeled field IDs,
option values, descriptions, image URLs, and a submission template with the actual field IDs.
Edit its placeholder values and run the displayed command to respond. `submit` takes a JSON object
keyed by field IDs; use option values for choices and arrays for multiple choices. Use
`qz submit TASK_ID -` to read answers from stdin. Invalid or stale submissions return the current
input and its template so you can correct the response directly.
`approve` continues a confirmation after you finish the requested action. `reject` declines the
current request; `cancel` stops the whole task.

Each response reads the current wait ID before sending. To answer a specific request you already
read, pass `--wait-id WAIT_ID` to `submit`, `approve`, or `reject`. A stale or invalid response
leaves the request pending. Review the application consent notice included in the pending input,
such as location sharing, before approving. A permission dialog the browser itself shows needs a
click in the qz side panel or sidebar. CLI approval reports that action is needed and preserves
the wait without opening a browser page.
With `--wait` or `--stream`, the command stays connected while you grant permission in the paired browser.
Location approval reads the current disclosure version and includes it in the response. Human
terminal output shows the notice before submitting the explicit approval; JSON output remains a
single final result. MCP callers should show the notice to the user before sending approval with
the returned `consentVersion`.

`submit`, `approve`, and `reject` accept `--wait` and `--stream` with the same completion condition:
the task has completed and its follow-up and steering queues are empty. They follow successive
runs, questions, and permission requests. Each new request is shown once. Respond in the side
panel, the Firefox sidebar, or another terminal; the original command continues automatically. `watch` follows an
existing task with this same condition without resubmitting anything. Timeouts and Ctrl-C stop
watching, while the task continues in the browser.

## Browser selection and MCP tools

Use `--client NAME|UUID` or `-c NAME|UUID` to select a browser. `qz browsers` lists registered names,
UUIDs, and online status. See [browser selection](#add-and-select-browsers) for pairing and name reuse.
Use `-t` for `--title`. Run `qz help COMMAND` or `qz COMMAND --help` for command-specific options.

The default MCP catalog is the direct-drive set: `qingzhou_guide`, `qingzhou_create_drive_session`,
`qingzhou_list_drive_sessions`, `qingzhou_get_drive_session`, `qingzhou_stop_session`,
`qingzhou_execute_tool`, `qingzhou_list_tools`, `qingzhou_get_tool`, and `qingzhou_bridge_status`.
`qingzhou_guide` returns the CLI workflow from `skills/qz-browser-agent/SKILL.md`.
MCP clients use the protocol below and [MCP connection setup](#connect-an-mcp-client).
Run `qz skill` for the guide shipped with the installed CLI.
`qz mcp` prints the local MCP endpoint. `qz mcp --profile full`
prints the task and diagnostic catalog. A direct-drive session lists all discoverable tools as compact signatures from
`qingzhou_list_tools`. `qingzhou_get_tool` returns the selected tool's full schema, and returns
`DRIVE_TOOL_FORBIDDEN` for a blocked name. Set `wait: false` to receive a job ID and read the
result with `qingzhou_get_tool_job`. The full catalog also provides `qingzhou_get_trace` and
`qingzhou_clear_trace` for diagnostics. MCP `qingzhou_list_tools` and `qingzhou_get_tool` can
inspect the base catalog without a session. To inspect loaded Skill tools by name, pass
`sessionId` to `qingzhou_get_tool`.
Tool execution requires a created session: omitting `sessionId` returns `DRIVE_SESSION_REQUIRED`;
an unknown ID returns `DRIVE_SESSION_NOT_FOUND`. Neither case creates a session. Check the browser selection and ID,
or create a new task session with `qz session create --title "Task title"` / `qingzhou_create_drive_session({title:"Task title"})`.

`qz session create --title "Task title"` creates a fresh session and requires a readable title.
It prints `sessionId <id>`; with `--json`, read `result.sessionId`. The new session activates the
tools of enabled user Global Skills; Resident Skills are always active, and Site Skills activate on
matching task sites. `result.qz_skills` lists the summaries of the Skills available to the new
session, in the same form as a script receipt's `context.qz_skills`, and is omitted when Skill
discovery is unavailable. `qz skills tools --session ID` shows each Skill's state. Use the installed `qz` command
and read `qz skill` for its guide. `qz session list` lists direct-drive sessions, and
`qz session show ID` reads `{sessionId,title,status}`. Finish with `qz session cancel ID` to end
the session and clean up its created tabs, including while a script is running. User tabs are
preserved. Add `--keep result --keep evidence` to return specific task pages to the user;
references are validated before stopping, and the first cancellation fixes the retention decision.
Further execution returns `DRIVE_SESSION_ENDED`.

`qz script --session ID [FILE|-] [--args JSON]` runs JavaScript outside the page. It reads a local
file or stdin; `--args` supplies the script's `args` value. Use the `qz` SDK: `qz.openTab(options)`
returns a Tab, `qz.tab(tabRef)` binds a Page, and `page.locator(targetOrQuery)` creates an element query.
Locator actions resolve a unique match and wait for it to become usable within one call budget.
Awaited SDK calls return business values directly and throw on failure.
For additional capabilities and active Skill tools, discover compact signatures with `qz.listTools()`
and selected full schemas with `qz.listTools({names:["list_images"]})`, then use `qz.call(name,args)`.
`qz.call("load_skill",{name})` activates that Skill's tools for the session immediately, including
later calls in the same script.
`page.evaluate(code,args?,options?)` runs a self-contained page function with DOM and login-state
access; pass its inputs explicitly and return JSON. Outer scripts survive page navigation;
an evaluation that unloads its own page can be interrupted. The
[installed Skill](../skills/qz-browser-agent/SKILL.md) provides the SDK reference and workflow.

Ctrl-C (`SIGINT`) or `SIGTERM` cancels the current script request, preserving its session and tabs.
Already-dispatched browser actions may still finish and are not undone. A supervisor should signal its owned CLI process or
process group; signaling an npm wrapper alone depends on its shell forwarding the signal.

```sh
qz session create --title "Read example page"
qz script --session SESSION_ID - <<'JS'
const { tabRef } = await qz.openTab({url:"https://example.com", tabAlias:"page"});
return await qz.tab(tabRef).read({limit:3000});
JS
qz session show SESSION_ID
qz session cancel SESSION_ID
```

stdout is JSON `{ok,result,trace}` on success and failure. `ok` reports execution success; `trace` is an ordered string array of errors and explicit `trace()`/`console` diagnostics without levels. `result` is the returned business value, `null` for `undefined`, or a failure in `{code,message,hint?,details?}` form. Business `trace`/`traces` fields stay inside `result`. Script locations are in `details`. Exit codes are `0` for success, `1` for execution or connection failure, and `2` for invalid arguments. `--timeout` defaults to `120` seconds, accepts `>0` through `3600`, and the request waits 60 seconds longer. The caller's deadline must allow that request to finish. A timeout does not undo completed browser actions.

For action-dependent navigation or popups, use `locator.click({waitFor:"navigation"})` or
`locator.click({waitFor:"popup"})`. The wait listens before dispatching the action once; failure
never replays it. For current element state, use `locator.wait({state:"visible"})`; for an exact
attached match count, use `locator.wait({count:3})`. `locator.count()` reads the current count.
Use `page.waitForFunction(code,args?,options?)` for application-specific completion conditions.

MCP clients can call `qingzhou_execute_tool` directly. Its single-call transport returns
`{toolName,sessionId,isError,result}`: inspect isError, then read result as the business value or
ToolError; script calls carry the `{ok,result,trace}` receipt in result. Do not infer execution status
from keys inside a script's returned object. Batches
correlate each result by call ID and are not transactions. The service extends script request
waiting to at least the execution budget plus 60 seconds without rewriting execution budgets.
Native MCP session operations include `qingzhou_list_drive_sessions`,
`qingzhou_get_drive_session` and `qingzhou_stop_session`.

A CLI process exiting does not close its session's tabs. While the extension runtime runs,
about 30 minutes of inactivity triggers cleanup. Cancel the session for task cleanup;
`qz cleanup` disconnects browsers from the local services. Full MCP can explicitly retain created tabs with
`qingzhou_stop_session({sessionId,keepTabs:true,cascade:false})`. Check the session and page
after an interrupted request before repeating an action; reconnecting does not replay it.

## Data, images, and Skills

```bash
qz data
qz data export TABLE
qz data export TABLE --format csv
qz data delete TABLE
qz images
qz images export COLLECTION
qz images delete COLLECTION
qz skills --query research
qz skills show NAME
qz skills read NAME scripts/run.js --limit 20000
qz skills tools --session TASK_ID
qz skills export NAME
```

Use the exact names printed by each list; quote names containing spaces. Data exports default to
Excel (`xlsx`); `--format csv` selects CSV. Image collections export as a ZIP containing available
image files and metadata. Missing local images are reported in the result. Skill exports contain
one user-installed Skill and its resources; built-in Skills require the extension and cannot be
exported independently.

`skills show` includes the resource paths. `skills read NAME PATH` reads one resource, with a
default limit of 20,000 characters. Use `--start` and `--limit` to select a chunk; truncated text
includes the command for the next chunk. `skills tools` lists contributed tools and whether they
are active in the selected task's context.
`skills --scope all|global|site|resident` filters by activation scope. Exports accept `--filename NAME`.
`automations --limit N` limits the automation list.

Exports use the browser's downloads. The result includes the download status, ID, filename, and path when
the browser provides it. Pending Chrome downloads are in `chrome://downloads`. Pending Firefox
downloads are in `about:downloads`. `delete` removes the named table
or image collection and its rows. Image blobs shared by other collections or task history remain
in the asset store.

## Settings and automations

```bash
qz settings
qz settings get model
qz settings set model MODEL_ID
qz settings set vision true
qz settings set '{"modelParameters":{"temperature":0.5}}'
qz settings set - < settings.json
qz automations
qz automations run AUTOMATION_ID
```

`settings` returns current values, editable fields, provider IDs, and protocol IDs. Credentials are
redacted; `qz settings get apiKey` reports whether a key is configured. `set KEY VALUE` parses JSON
values such as booleans, numbers, objects, and arrays; other values are strings. `set JSON` applies
a patch containing the supplied top-level fields. Follow the field descriptions for values that
replace an entire object, such as `modelParameters`.

Read credential patches from stdin to keep them out of shell history. JSON is validated before
connecting. The extension validates field names and values before saving. Browser commands accept
`--client NAME|UUID` to select a profile. `automations run` starts an existing automation and
returns its task ID.

The CLI uses the same browser operations as MCP. Its commands correspond to tasks, data,
images, Skills, settings, and automations. `qz mcp` only returns the connection URL for MCP
clients.

## Terminal output

Interactive terminals show readable text; pipes and redirected output receive JSON. Use `--json`
to request JSON explicitly or `--plain` to keep text when redirecting output. `--no-color` or the
`NO_COLOR` environment variable disables color. `qz mcp` prints only the MCP URL by default;
`qz mcp --json` returns a JSON result.

In JSON mode, `--wait` and `--stream` emit one final JSON result on stdout. Complete pending-input
notices and submission templates appear on stderr so you can respond while preserving
machine-readable output. MCP snapshots and rejected responses include `input`, with a
`responseTemplate` that binds answers to the current session and wait. A permission dialog the
browser itself shows provides user instructions instead of an approval template.
Exit codes are `0` for success (including reading pending input), `1` for an operation or
task failure or a rejected submission, `2` for invalid arguments, and `130` for Ctrl-C.
Connection errors include the GitHub setup guide and installation link.

## Local access

The service accepts connections only on your computer. Ordinary websites cannot use its MCP
endpoint. Local programs can control connected qz tasks while the service is running.
Run `qz cleanup` to stop local services and disconnect their browser and MCP connections;
side-panel tasks keep running, while active direct-drive scripts are interrupted.

Connection settings and browser registrations are stored in `~/.qz-browser-agent/run/`.
Pairing credentials stay on your computer and are omitted from status output.

Tests need Python 3.11+, uv, and the Chromium version installed by Playwright:

```bash
npx playwright install chromium
npm run doctor
npm test
```

On Linux, `npx playwright install-deps chromium` installs missing browser system libraries. These
tests use synthetic data and local services.

To work on one part of the project:

```bash
npm test -- unit contracts
npm test -- unit --match session
npm test -- browser --list
npm test -- playwright renderer-lifecycle.spec.mjs --workers 1
npm test -- grid
```

`npm run verify` runs `unit`, `contracts`, and `services` after typecheck. Those suites are shared:
they do not load `dist/extension/` or `dist/extension-firefox/` as the package under test.
`npm run verify:chrome` runs `browser`, `e2e`, `release`, and `visual`. Those suites load the Chrome
package. `npm test` still defaults to `unit`, `contracts`, `services`, and `browser`. `--all` selects
the shared suites plus the Chrome package suites. `--match` filters unit filenames or suite commands.
`--list` shows what would run. `browser` includes Chromium Playwright, Python page smoke tests, and
Data Grid tests. `playwright` runs only that Chromium Playwright config and accepts its own options.
`npm test`, `npm run verify`, and `npm run verify:chrome` do not select the Firefox suite and do not
launch Firefox.

### Firefox package

`npm run verify:firefox` is the Firefox package suite. It type-checks, builds
`dist/extension-firefox/` in development mode, runs `tests/unit/test-firefox-*.mjs`, and runs
Playwright against that directory in Mozilla Firefox. `npm run build:firefox` writes the production
package and does not run the suite. The Firefox tests run from `npm run verify:firefox` or
`npm test -- firefox`. `npm run verify` and `npm run verify:chrome` do not launch Firefox.

Ordinary changes finish on typecheck plus focused tests. When a change carries broad or
browser-specific risk, this table shows which suite covers it:

| Change at risk | Suite |
| --- | --- |
| Shared runtime, manifest, locales, content scripts, or `scripts/build-extension.mjs` | `npm run verify`; add `npm run verify:firefox` when Firefox behavior is at risk |
| Chrome side panel, Playwright, e2e, release, or visual behavior loaded from `dist/extension/` | `npm run verify:chrome` |
| `src/background/firefox/**`, `src/sidepanel/firefox/**`, `firefox-boot.ts`, `scripts/firefox-manifest.mjs`, `tests/firefox/**`, `tests/unit/test-firefox-*.mjs` | `npm test -- unit --match firefox`; `npm run verify:firefox` when the Firefox package is at risk |

Install Mozilla Firefox 154 or newer, including its system libraries:

```bash
npx playwright install firefox
npx playwright install-deps firefox
```

The suite launches that binary headless on Firefox's WebDriver BiDi channel (`moz-firefox`) and
passes `executablePath`. It does not launch Chromium. Set `FIREFOX_EXECUTABLE` to choose a binary.
Otherwise the locator uses `firefox` on `PATH`, then a Firefox build from `npx playwright install
firefox` whose `--version` prints `Mozilla Firefox` 139 or newer, then
`/tmp/ff/firefox/firefox`, `/usr/bin/firefox`, and `/snap/bin/firefox`. A missing binary stops the
suite with those install commands in the error. Set `QINGZHOU_FIREFOX_HEADED=1` to show the window.
`QINGZHOU_FIREFOX_PLAYWRIGHT_WORKERS` bounds that Playwright process; it does not read
`QINGZHOU_PLAYWRIGHT_WORKERS`.

```bash
npm run verify:firefox
npm test -- firefox
```

The Playwright file temporarily installs `dist/extension-firefox/`. It checks that the toolbar
button and the `_execute_sidebar_action` shortcut open Firefox's sidebar, and that no tab is
`moz-extension://…/sidepanel.html`. In light, dark, a macOS accent, and a temporary theme add-on,
it measures text contrast of at least 4.5:1 and icon and focus-ring contrast of at least 3:1 in
each control state, and checks the disabled primary and send buttons. It checks horizontal overflow
at 320 and 400 pixels and `notifications.create` with and without `requireInteraction`. A
`sidePanel.open()` call outside a user gesture must log Firefox's error and set the `!` badge and
the hint notification. A notification click must not create a second notification, and opening
the sidebar by shortcut, switcher, or toolbar must clear the badge.

Reports go to `tests/results/playwright-firefox/` and `tests/results/firefox-suite.json`. The JSON
record names `browser=firefox` and `package=dist/extension-firefox`. The Chromium Playwright report
stays in `tests/results/playwright-report/`. A log line at the start of each suite names the browser
and package. `QINGZHOU_PLAYWRIGHT_CHANNEL` cannot point the Chromium suites at Firefox.

Choose checks by the size of the change:

- Small changes (copy and i18n text, timeouts, thresholds, gates, small fixes, documentation) run
  no test suites. Run `npm run typecheck` when TypeScript changed and it is cheap.
- Ordinary feature and bug work runs `npm run typecheck` plus focused tests for the touched area,
  such as `npm test -- unit --match <area>` or `npm test -- playwright <spec files>`. It does not
  finish with a full suite run.
- Broad changes to shared contracts, or a task that asks for it, run `npm run verify`. Add
  `npm run verify:chrome` or `npm run verify:firefox` only for risky changes specific to that
  package. For a Chrome run, set `QINGZHOU_PLAYWRIGHT_WORKERS` to the available core count
  (`$(nproc)` on Linux).
- `npm run verify:coverage` runs for releases or an explicit request for coverage gates. For
  narrower coverage checks, use `npm test -- unit --coverage`.

Capture a long run's output and exit code on the first run, for example
`npm run verify:chrome > /tmp/verify-chrome.log 2>&1; echo EXIT:$?`, and cite that log instead of
rerunning. On a busy machine,
`npm test -- --all --jobs 1` runs the shared and Chrome suites sequentially.

Reports go to `tests/results/`. Use `npm test -- report` to open the Playwright report, or `npm test
-- behavior --journey H03,A07` to run the tests linked to those entries in the [behavior
index](../tests/BEHAVIOR_INDEX.md). See [tests/README.md](../tests/README.md) for details.
